item.title: Hiroshima Oysters: Japan's Great Oyster Coast — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima is Japan’s oyster capital, growing the great majority of the country’s crop on rafts strung across the calm, nutrient-rich waters of the Seto Inland Sea. The oysters here are famously plump and creamy, and locals eat them in every conceivable way: grilled in the half shell over charcoal at stalls on Miyajima, deep-fried as kaki-fry, simmered in a miso hotpot called doteni, folded into rice, or simply raw with lemon.

item.title: Miyajima & Itsukushima Shrine: The Floating Torii — Guide
item.description: Miyajima, officially Itsukushima, is a small sacred island in the Seto Inland Sea just off Hiroshima and one of the most beautiful places in Japan. Its centrepiece is Itsukushima Shrine, a vermilion complex built out over the water on wooden piles so that at high tide it appears to float, and its huge O-torii gate, standing offshore, rises straight from the sea — one of the country’s three most celebrated views and a World Heritage Site.

item.title: Miyajima Autumn Foliage: Momijidani in Flame — Guide
item.description: Miyajima is famous for its maples — the island’s signature sweet, momiji manju, is even shaped like a maple leaf — and each autumn Momijidani, the ‘maple valley’ behind Itsukushima Shrine, becomes one of the most beautiful places in western Japan. Hundreds of maple trees, planted over centuries, turn brilliant shades of red, orange and gold in November, framing a small park of stone bridges, a mountain stream and the lower station of the Mount Misen ropeway.

item.title: Momiji Manju: Miyajima's Maple-Leaf Cakes — Guide
item.description: Momiji manju are little cakes baked in the shape of a maple leaf, a nod to the maples of Momijidani, and they are the definitive souvenir of Hiroshima. Created on Miyajima over a century ago, they are made from a light castella-style sponge batter poured into leaf-shaped moulds and filled traditionally with sweet red bean paste, though modern fillings run to custard, chocolate, matcha and cheese. On Miyajima you can watch them being made on rotating griddles and eat them still warm, which is a completely different experience from the boxed ones — and several shops sell them battered and deep-fried on a stick as age-momiji.

item.title: Mount Misen: Miyajima's Sacred Summit — Guide
item.description: Mount Misen, the 535-metre peak that rises behind Itsukushima Shrine, is the sacred heart of Miyajima and the island’s finest walk. Revered for over a thousand years and covered in primeval forest, its trails climb through temples and past a hall holding a flame said to have burned continuously since the monk Kukai lit it in the ninth century — the same flame used to light the Flame of Peace in Hiroshima.

item.title: Best Hotels & Ryokan in Hiroshima: From Luxury Miyajima to Onomichi U2
item.description: Hiroshima’s accommodation landscape is more varied than the city’s reputation suggests. Central Hiroshima offers reliable international and Japanese business hotels well-positioned for Peace Park and the Shinkansen station. Miyajima island has a handful of historic ryokan with private onsen and views of the Inland Sea — among western Japan’s finest stays. Onomichi’s converted-warehouse Hotel Cycle and the Setoda island’s design-led Azumi Setoda are two of the most stylish small-luxury hotels in Japan.

item.title: Hiroshima Family Trip Guide: Miyajima Deer, Peace Park & Inland Sea Adventures
item.description: Hiroshima is one of the easier Japanese prefectures to visit with children. The headline attractions — Miyajima’s wild deer, the floating torii gate, a samurai castle, a baseball stadium, the Mazda factory tour, the Shimanami Kaido cycling route — work well across age ranges. The compact city centre means short tram rides between sights, and the city’s reputation for friendly, English-tolerant service makes navigation gentler than Tokyo or Kyoto. This guide covers age-appropriate planning, kid-friendly food, and the practical logistics of travelling with children in Hiroshima Prefecture.

item.title: Hiroshima Girls Trip Guide: Onomichi Cats, Oyster Bars & Miyajima Ryokan
item.description: Hiroshima has the makings of an excellent girls trip — a photogenic floating shrine, a chic ryokan island, hillside temple towns with cat-friendly cafes, lemon-scented spa products from the Setouchi islands, and three days' worth of oyster lunches. The pace is gentler than Tokyo or Osaka, the food is built around small luxuries (fresh oysters, momiji manju, sake tastings), and the photogenic spots are not yet overrun by Instagram tourism. This guide is your three-to-five day Hiroshima girls trip blueprint.

item.title: Hiroshima Goshuin Guide: Itsukushima Shrine, Gokoku Shrine & Temple Seals
item.description: A goshuin (御朱印) is a calligraphic stamp issued by a Shinto shrine or Buddhist temple, hand-written on a folding accordion-style book called a goshuin-cho (御朱印帳). Originally a receipt issued to pilgrims who had copied sutras at a temple, goshuin have become one of the most rewarding souvenirs of a Japan trip — each one is hand-brushed individually, beautifully personal, and impossible to mass-produce. Hiroshima Prefecture is an excellent place to start (or continue) collecting: Itsukushima Shrine issues one of Japan’s most prized goshuin, and the prefecture offers a manageable circuit of major and minor shrines and temples on a single trip.

item.title: Hiroshima Nature Guide: Miyajima, Shimanami Kaido & Taishakukyo Gorge
item.description: Most visitors arrive in Hiroshima expecting a city, and leave surprised by the breadth of its natural landscape. The prefecture stretches from the islands of the Seto Inland Sea up to the mountainous border with Shimane, and along the way passes a sacred forest mountain, two world-class gorges, an island-hopping cycling route considered among the best in Asia, and dozens of small islands with their own micro-cultures of citrus, fishing, and slow time.

item.title: Hiroshima Sightseeing Guide: Peace Memorial, Miyajima & Hiroshima Castle
item.description: Hiroshima is one of those rare cities where the sightseeing list is short, the depth is enormous, and the contrast between sites is dramatic. The Peace Memorial Park and the Atomic Bomb Dome ask you to slow down and confront one of the twentieth century’s most consequential moments. An hour later, a ferry deposits you at Miyajima, where a vermillion torii gate stands in the sea and wild deer wander between thousand-year-old shrine pavilions.

item.title: Hiroshima Food Guide: Okonomiyaki, Oysters, Anago Rice & More
item.description: Hiroshima has one of the most distinctive regional food identities in Japan. Where Osaka’s okonomiyaki is mixed together and cooked as a single mass, Hiroshima’s is built in layers — crepe batter, a mountain of shredded cabbage, pork belly, yakisoba noodles, and a fried egg on top, assembled on a teppan griddle with the precision of a craftsman. This difference is not minor: Hiroshima locals will defend the superiority of their style with considerable conviction.
